To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
focal brain ischemia and CSD lead to a massive induction of G-CSF mRNA in the ischemic and nonischemic hemisphere.
G-CSF is induced in the brain after focal cerebral ischemia or CSD.

G-CSF is strongly induced in focal cerebral ischemia, that this induction is not restricted to ischemic tissue but also involves remote nonischemically damaged brain regions, that periinfarct cortical spreading depolarizations are the most likely trigger for this response, and that G-CSF mRNA levels in ischemic tissue are higher than in nonischemic areas.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the induction of granuleocyte colony-stimulatig factor in the brain.
the role of G-CSF in brain ischemia.
the role of hematopoietic cytokines, such as granulocyte colony stimulating factor (G-CSf) and granulocyte-macrophage colony stimulating factor (GM-CSF), in brain ischemia.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
CSD induces G-CSF mRNA, and this induction is not restricted to the ischemic core but also occurs in nonischemic tissue.
the G-CSF gene is induced in ischemic lesions and remote nonischaemic brain regions after photochemically induced and permanent focal ischemia, and after CSD.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
G-CSF is induced after ischemia, but that the induction is mediated by NMDA receptor activation and CSD, and that the induction is restricted to the ischemic lesion and the remote periinfarct zone.
G-CSF is induced by ischemic brain damage and that CSD is a trigger of this process.
